node-1.label: A woman in her 60s presented with a new pruritic rash

node-2.label: The rash initially developed on the patient's legs 13 days before presentation and subsequently progressed to her feet, arms, hands, and trunk; associated symptoms included a burning sensation and occasional pain.

node-3.label: Physical examination showed numerous erythematous edematous coalescing papules and plaques on the upper and lower extremities and scattered erythematous papules and plaques on the back and buttocks; some plaques were annular and polycyclic in configuration with central hyperpigmentation, while the chest, abdomen, face, and oral mucosa were clear.

node-4.label: Medical history was notable for endometrial adenocarcinoma status post hysterectomy and recent postoperative radiotherapy totaling 50.4 Gy in 28 fractioned doses, completed 4 days after the onset of the rash.

node-5.label: The patient denied any new medications, exposure to chemotherapy, imaging with intravenous contrast, or recent travel; the remainder of her review of systems was unremarkable.

why.why: The newly explicit finding that the biopsy lacks typical radiation-induced changes further undermines radiation-related dermatitis. Expert analyses agree that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without radiation changes and the widespread annular/polycyclic morphology outside the radiation field do not support this diagnosis. The only supporting feature is recent radiotherapy, so confidence is lowered to 0.02.

The patient denied new medications, contrast exposure, or travel, and expert analyses agree that drug/contact hypersensitivity is unlikely based on histopathologic and clinical findings. With no exogenous trigger identified, hypersensitivity is very unlikely, so confidence is lowered to 0.05.

Laboratory and pathology expert analyses both affirm that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis and 11% peripheral eosinophilia, in the absence of exogenous triggers and with a recent endometrial adenocarcinoma history, strongly support a paraneoplastic/autoimmune process. Radiation dermatitis, drug/contact hypersensitivity, and urticarial vasculitis are explicitly excluded. Pending serologic markers do not weaken this conclusion, so confidence is raised to 0.9.

node-9.label: Skin biopsy shows dense perivascular and interstitial infiltrate with innumerable eosinophils, without leukocytoclasia or erythrocyte extravasation.

node-11.label: The rash is a paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis

why.why: The newly added explicit finding that the biopsy lacks typical radiation changes strengthens the case for paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis. Both pathologist and laboratory physician analyses affirm that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis, 11% peripheral eosinophilia, recent endometrial adenocarcinoma, and absence of new medications or exposures all point to this diagnosis. Confidence is raised to 0.85; pending serologic markers, tumor staging, and infection/hematologic exclusion prevent a higher value.

Expert analyses confirm that urticarial vasculitis lacks histologic support: the biopsy shows no leukocytoclasia or erythrocyte extravasation. The clinical morphology alone is insufficient, so confidence is lowered to 0.03.

node-14.label: Tumor staging and radiotherapy details have not been obtained

node-15.label: Infection and hematologic disorders have not been excluded

node-16.label: Paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis associated with endometrial adenocarcinoma

why.why: The biopsy shows a dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis or radiation changes, and peripheral eosinophilia is 11%, in the setting of recent endometrial adenocarcinoma and no new medications or exposures. Both pathologist and laboratory physician analyses strongly support paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis associated with this malignancy. Confidence is raised to 0.85; pending serologic markers, staging details, and infection/hematologic workup keep it from being higher.

node-17.label: Autoimmune eosinophilic dermatosis (e.g., eosinophilic annular erythema)

attrs.why: The current frontier 'Paraneoplastic/autoimmune' can be refined into a purely autoimmune subtype. The annular/polycyclic morphology and eosinophilic infiltrate are compatible with autoimmune eosinophilic dermatoses, but the strong temporal association with endometrial adenocarcinoma and lack of serologic autoimmune markers make this less likely than a paraneoplastic process.

node-18.label: Eosinophilic dermatosis secondary to occult hematologic disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome

attrs.why: The current frontier 'Paraneoplastic/autoimmune' does not fully cover hematologic causes of eosinophilia. Peripheral eosinophilia of 11% and dense eosinophilic skin infiltration could be explained by an occult hematologic disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome, which has not yet been excluded. This candidate represents a necessary refinement because infection and hematologic disorders remain pending in the belief/graph.

node-19.label: Skin biopsy shows no typical radiation-induced changes (e.g., epidermal atrophy, telangiectasia, atypical fibroblasts)

node-20.label: Eosinophilic dermatosis secondary to occult infection

attrs.why: Infection has not been excluded and can cause peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic skin infiltration, but the patient had no fever, travel, or exposure history and denied new medications, making this far less likely than paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis. Confidence is low at 0.05.

node-4.label: Medical history was notable for endometrial adenocarcinoma status post hysterectomy and recent postoperative radiotherapy totaling 50.4 Gy in 28 fractioned doses, completed 4 days after the onset of the rash.

node-5.label: The patient denied any new medications, exposure to chemotherapy, imaging with intravenous contrast, or recent travel; the remainder of her review of systems was unremarkable.

why.why: The newly explicit finding that the biopsy lacks typical radiation-induced changes further undermines radiation-related dermatitis. Expert analyses agree that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without radiation changes and the widespread annular/polycyclic morphology outside the radiation field do not support this diagnosis. The only supporting feature is recent radiotherapy, so confidence is lowered to 0.02.

The patient denied new medications, contrast exposure, or travel, and expert analyses agree that drug/contact hypersensitivity is unlikely based on histopathologic and clinical findings. With no exogenous trigger identified, hypersensitivity is very unlikely, so confidence is lowered to 0.05.

Laboratory and pathology expert analyses both affirm that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis and 11% peripheral eosinophilia, in the absence of exogenous triggers and with a recent endometrial adenocarcinoma history, strongly support a paraneoplastic/autoimmune process. Radiation dermatitis, drug/contact hypersensitivity, and urticarial vasculitis are explicitly excluded. Pending serologic markers do not weaken this conclusion, so confidence is raised to 0.9.

node-9.label: Skin biopsy shows dense perivascular and interstitial infiltrate with innumerable eosinophils, without leukocytoclasia or erythrocyte extravasation.

node-11.label: The rash is a paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis

why.why: The newly added explicit finding that the biopsy lacks typical radiation changes strengthens the case for paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis. Both pathologist and laboratory physician analyses affirm that the dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis, 11% peripheral eosinophilia, recent endometrial adenocarcinoma, and absence of new medications or exposures all point to this diagnosis. Confidence is raised to 0.85; pending serologic markers, tumor staging, and infection/hematologic exclusion prevent a higher value.

Expert analyses confirm that urticarial vasculitis lacks histologic support: the biopsy shows no leukocytoclasia or erythrocyte extravasation. The clinical morphology alone is insufficient, so confidence is lowered to 0.03.

node-14.label: Tumor staging and radiotherapy details have not been obtained

node-15.label: Infection and hematologic disorders have not been excluded

node-16.label: Paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis associated with endometrial adenocarcinoma

why.why: The biopsy shows a dense eosinophilic infiltrate without vasculitis or radiation changes, and peripheral eosinophilia is 11%, in the setting of recent endometrial adenocarcinoma and no new medications or exposures. Both pathologist and laboratory physician analyses strongly support paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis associated with this malignancy. Confidence is raised to 0.85; pending serologic markers, staging details, and infection/hematologic workup keep it from being higher.

node-17.label: Autoimmune eosinophilic dermatosis (e.g., eosinophilic annular erythema)

attrs.why: The current frontier 'Paraneoplastic/autoimmune' can be refined into a purely autoimmune subtype. The annular/polycyclic morphology and eosinophilic infiltrate are compatible with autoimmune eosinophilic dermatoses, but the strong temporal association with endometrial adenocarcinoma and lack of serologic autoimmune markers make this less likely than a paraneoplastic process.

node-18.label: Eosinophilic dermatosis secondary to occult hematologic disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome

attrs.why: The current frontier 'Paraneoplastic/autoimmune' does not fully cover hematologic causes of eosinophilia. Peripheral eosinophilia of 11% and dense eosinophilic skin infiltration could be explained by an occult hematologic disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome, which has not yet been excluded. This candidate represents a necessary refinement because infection and hematologic disorders remain pending in the belief/graph.

node-19.label: Skin biopsy shows no typical radiation-induced changes (e.g., epidermal atrophy, telangiectasia, atypical fibroblasts)

node-20.label: Eosinophilic dermatosis secondary to occult infection

attrs.why: Infection has not been excluded and can cause peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic skin infiltration, but the patient had no fever, travel, or exposure history and denied new medications, making this far less likely than paraneoplastic eosinophilic dermatosis. Confidence is low at 0.05.
